Class enumeration in mixture models

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/class-enumeration.Rmd
class-enumeration.Rmd

Finite mixture models represent population heterogeneity as a small number of unobserved subpopulations, the latent classes, each characterized by its own distribution of the observed indicators (McLachlan and Peel, 2000). In latent profile analysis the class-specific parameters are the means and variances of continuous indicators; in latent class analysis they are the response probabilities of categorical indicators. When observations are nested within higher-level units, the units may themselves differ in the distribution of classes. In the data used here, course enrolments are nested within students, and students differ in the proportion of their enrolments that show a given pattern of engagement. The two-level mixture model of Vermunt (2003) represents this variation with a second, higher-level latent variable whose categories, the group classes, are defined by their distributions over the lower-level profiles. For a fixed number of classes, estimation yields the class sizes and the class-specific parameters. The number of classes, however, is not a parameter of the model: it is specified before estimation, at both levels in a two-level model, and every subsequent inference is conditional on that specification.

Determining the number of classes is difficult because each conventional criterion for model comparison is deficient in a specific respect. The maximized likelihood is non-decreasing in the number of classes, since a model with k + 1 classes contains the model with k classes as a special case. The likelihood ratio test of k against k + 1 classes does not have its usual chi-square reference distribution, because the null hypothesis places a mixing proportion on the boundary of the parameter space and leaves the parameters of the omitted class unidentified (McLachlan and Peel, 2000). Valid p-values can be obtained by parametric bootstrap (McLachlan, 1987), at the cost of refitting both models to many simulated data sets. Information criteria avoid hypothesis testing by penalizing the deviance for the number of estimated parameters; criteria with a weaker penalty, such as the Akaike information criterion, select more classes than criteria with a stronger penalty, such as the Bayesian information criterion (Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén, 2007).

Applied data introduce further complications. In large samples the Bayesian information criterion frequently continues to decrease as classes are added, because minor misspecifications become detectable and each additional class absorbs part of them. The minimum then falls at the largest model fitted, and the magnitude of successive improvements is more informative than the location of the minimum. In a two-level model the numbers of lower- and higher-level classes must be determined jointly, and the penalty of the Bayesian information criterion depends on whether the sample size is taken as the number of higher-level units or of lower-level observations (Lukočienė, Varriale and Vermunt, 2010). Moreover, a model may fit well yet separate its classes poorly, and the reported solution may be a local rather than the global maximum of the likelihood.

This article applies class enumeration to a two-level latent profile model. All combinations of the specified numbers of profiles and group classes are estimated with enumerate_classes(), and every fitted model is retained. Each candidate is characterized by its information criteria under both definitions of the sample size, by the change in a criterion with each additional profile and group class, by the knee of each resulting curve, by the certainty of its classification and by diagnostics of its estimation. Selected candidates are then compared directly, and the chosen candidate is extracted for substantive analysis.

The full evidence is reported because no single statistic determines the number of classes. Considered jointly, the criteria, the changes between neighbouring candidates and the indices of classification quality indicate where additional classes cease to improve the model, and a decision based on them can be stated, justified and reproduced from the reported tables. Model selection defines each source of evidence and discusses its interpretation and limitations.

library(latents)

Data

The examples use course_engagement, a long-format data frame with one row per course enrolment, comprising 1,422 enrolments of 106 students. Five measures of course activity serve as indicators: browsing of the course site, lecture viewing, forum reading, forum posting and attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course, so that zero denotes the course mean. The column student identifies the student to whom each enrolment belongs.

head(course_engagement)

#> 5 disengaged     wavering

Because enrolments are nested within students, the profiles describe patterns of activity within a single course, and the group classes describe students by the distribution of their enrolments over those patterns.

Fitting the candidate models

enumerate_classes() takes the data, the indicators (vars) and the group identifier (id). The arguments n_profiles and n_group_classes specify the numbers of classes to be considered, and one model is estimated for each combination; here the number of profiles ranges from one to six and the number of group classes from one to four. The argument model specifies the within-profile covariance structure. "VVI" assigns each profile its own variances and constrains the covariances to zero; when model is omitted, the four basic structures are estimated for every combination.

The likelihood of a mixture model is multimodal, so each model is estimated from several random starts and the solution with the highest likelihood is retained. The number of starts is set by n_starts, which, like every other estimation argument, applies identically to all candidates. Three starts per model are used here to limit computation; applied analyses should use at least ten, and a grid is re-estimated in its entirety when more starts are required, so that every candidate has the same opportunity to reach its maximum. The argument seed makes the starts reproducible. When many starts are used, a candidate with more profiles than the data support can reach a degenerate solution in which one profile collapses on a single observation with every variance at its lower bound; its likelihood, and hence its criteria, then depend on min_variance rather than on the data. boundary = "exclude" sets such starts aside for every candidate (see Diagnostics of the estimation).

activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models

The result contains 24 candidates. Each is named by its numbers of profiles and group classes (profiles4_groups3 denotes four profiles and three group classes), and this name identifies the candidate in all subsequent functions. The 3 candidates with a single profile and more than one group class are not identified: group classes are defined by differences in the distribution of profiles, and with a single profile no such differences exist. These candidates are retained in the table together with the error that terminated their estimation.

The columns form the following groups.

Columns Content
candidate, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model Identity of the candidate
log_likelihood, n_parameters Fit and size
aic, kic, bic_*, sabic_*, caic_*, awe_*, icl_*, clc_* Information criteria
profile_entropy, group_entropy Relative entropy at each level
avepp_min, avepp_max, avepp_mean, avepp_below Average posterior probability of the profiles
group_avepp_min, group_avepp_max, group_avepp_mean, group_avepp_below Average posterior probability of the group classes
converged, boundary, n_best_replicated, warnings, error Diagnostics of the estimation

Information criteria

An information criterion is the deviance, minus twice the maximized log-likelihood, plus a penalty for the estimated parameters; lower values indicate a more favourable balance of fit and complexity. In a two-level model the penalty of several criteria depends on the sample size. Criteria with the suffix _groups treat the 106 students as the independent units, and criteria with the suffix _individual the 1,422 enrolments (Lukočienė, Varriale and Vermunt, 2010). A single convention should be used throughout an analysis.

The candidate that minimizes each criterion:

get_results(models, "best")
#>    criterion  convention         candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value

#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles4_groups4          4               4   VVI 16769

#> 9        awe      groups profiles3_groups2          3               2   VVI 17169
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups3          2               3   VVI 17398
#> 11       icl      groups profiles4_groups2          4               2   VVI 16881
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 17140
#> 13       clc      groups profiles6_groups4          6               4   VVI 16580
#> 14       clc individuals profiles2_groups4          2               4   VVI 16944

The criteria do not agree. With students as the units, the Bayesian information criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978) is minimized by profiles4_groups3, the integrated completed likelihood (ICL; Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert, 2000) by profiles4_groups2 and the approximate weight of evidence (AWE; Banfield and Raftery, 1993) by profiles3_groups2. With enrolments as the units, BIC is minimized by profiles3_groups3. The Akaike information criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974) is minimized by profiles6_groups4, the largest candidate, because its weak penalty leaves it decreasing over the entire range. ICL and AWE penalize classification uncertainty in addition to the number of parameters and therefore favour fewer, better separated classes.

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, with one line per number of group classes and the minimum of each criterion circled.

plot(models)

A minimum at the largest number of profiles or group classes considered indicates that the criterion is still decreasing at the boundary of the grid, which should then be extended until the minimum is interior. Any criterion can be plotted by name, and what = "all" plots all of them.

plot(models, what = "bic_groups")

The clustering tree (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018) shows how the profiles divide as their number increases: each profile of a model is linked to the profiles of the next larger model that receive its observations.

plot(models, what = "tree")

Change with each additional class

When a criterion decreases over the entire range, the magnitude of each decrease constitutes the evidence. For each candidate, the table reports the decrease in BIC relative to the candidate with one profile fewer and the same number of group classes, and relative to the candidate with one group class fewer and the same number of profiles. A positive value indicates that the additional class lowered the criterion. Another criterion is selected with using.

With three group classes, a third profile lowers BIC by 85 and a fourth by 22, whereas a fifth raises it by 27, which the table reports as a negative decrease. The decreases are plotted in both directions, along the number of profiles (left) and along the number of group classes (right).

plot(models, what = "deltas")

The knee summary rescales both axes of a curve to the unit interval and identifies the candidate at the greatest perpendicular distance below the chord joining the first and last points. The rule follows the geometric definition of Kneedle (Satopää et al., 2011) without its smoothing and sensitivity threshold. A nearly linear curve yields a small maximum distance, so the reported distance indicates the strength of the bend as well as its location. Knees are computed along the number of profiles for each number of group classes, along the number of group classes for each number of profiles, and across all candidates ordered by their number of parameters.

get_results(models, "knees")

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is profiles4_groups3. Because the chord terminates at the largest candidate, the knee depends on the range of the grid; with the largest candidate omitted it is profiles3_groups3, as recorded in the columns stable and note. Along the number of group classes with four profiles, the knee is profiles4_groups2.

The criterion across all candidates simultaneously, expressed as the distance of each from the minimum:

plot(models, what = "heatmap")

Classification quality

Each observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class. Relative entropy (Ramaswamy et al., 1993) summarizes these probabilities over all observations; it equals 0 when every observation is equally likely to belong to every class and 1 when every observation is assigned to one class with certainty. The average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that class among the observations modally assigned to it (Nagin, 2005). Values of at least 0.7 to 0.8 are conventionally regarded as indicating adequate separation. The table of candidates reports the minimum, maximum and mean AvePP at each level and the number of classes below a cutoff, 0.8 by default, which is set with cutoff.

plot(models, what = "diagnostics")

The AvePP of every class of every candidate, together with its size and the relative entropy of its level:

For profiles4_groups3, the relative entropy is 0.74 for the profiles and 0.82 for the group classes; the minimum AvePP is 0.8 among the profiles and 0.87 among the group classes.

Diagnostics of the estimation

A maximum reached from several random starts is more credible than one reached once, since a single start may terminate at a local maximum. An estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, such as a variance at its lower bound, indicates a model too complex for the data, and a class containing a very small proportion of the observations is difficult to interpret and to replicate. The following plots report these diagnostics for every candidate.

plot(models, what = "trust")

plot(models, what = "smallest")

plot(models, what = "selection") displays all plots relevant to the choice of the number of classes jointly.

A candidate on a boundary whose smallest profile holds about one observation is a degenerate solution, not a profile: a Gaussian profile centred on one observation raises the likelihood without limit as its variances shrink, so the reported likelihood is fixed by min_variance. The default, boundary = "allow", reports it, as Mplus does, with a warning. boundary = "exclude" retains for each candidate the best start with no variance at its lower bound, and is advisable when many starts are used, since each additional start increases the chance of reaching such a solution. Categorical indicators are unaffected.

models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:5, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 200,
                            boundary = "exclude", seed = 1)

Comparing candidates

compare_models() tabulates selected candidates side by side. Candidates are specified by name, by their numbers of classes, or by a number of profiles or group classes. The comparison adds the difference in BIC from the minimum among the compared candidates and the BIC weight, exp(-delta_bic / 2) normalized to sum to one, which approximates the posterior probability of each candidate under equal prior probabilities (Wagenmakers and Farrell, 2004).

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

compare_models(models, bic_groups_pick, icl_groups_pick, awe_groups_pick)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model              Profiles  Group classes   k    LogLik       BIC   ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8  Group entropy  Group min AvePP

The same candidates specified by their numbers of classes, with labels:

compare_models(models, bic = c(4, 3), icl = c(4, 2), awe = c(3, 2))

Analysis of the chosen candidate

The analysis proceeds with profiles4_groups3, the candidate that minimizes BIC with students as the units. It is extracted by name with get_candidate(); specifying the numbers of classes, as in get_candidate(models, 4, 3), returns the same model.

chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen

The profiles are displayed as their means on the five indicators.

plot_profiles(chosen)

Each group class has its own distribution over the four profiles.

plot_prevalence(chosen)

The classification diagnostics of the chosen model:

diagnostics(chosen)

#> Classification quality: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> 
#>   Relative entropy     individuals 0.739    groups 0.823
#>   Smallest class       individuals 202.2 (14.2%)    groups 27.4 (25.8%)
#>   Lowest avg posterior individuals 0.801    groups 0.874
#>   Largest residual     -0.115  (lectures, forum_post; profile_3)
#> 
#> Tables: get_results(x, what = "entropy" | "classification" | 
#>         "average_posteriors" | "residuals" | "all"). plot(x) draws them.
plot_diagnostics(chosen)

With two or more group classes, the four views for the enrolments in their profiles are followed by the same views for the students in their group classes. Because a student is classified from all of their enrolments jointly, the group classes are typically far better separated than the profiles. A single view is selected with what, for example plot_diagnostics(chosen, what = "group_posteriors").

Each enrolment with its modal profile, the group class of its student and its posterior probabilities:

The profiles can be related to external variables. The mean of previous_grade in each profile is estimated with three_step(), which corrects for classification error by the BCH method (Bolck, Croon and Hagenaars, 2004; Vermunt, 2010).

three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
#> Distal outcome by class (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class   Mean          95% CI     SE  Effective n
#> -----  -----  --------------  -----  -----------
#>     1   0.17  [ 0.07,  0.27]  0.050       338.59
#>     2  -0.30  [-0.41, -0.18]  0.058       255.57

#>     4   0.32  [ 0.18,  0.45]  0.069       210.39

Testing neighbouring candidates

The bootstrap likelihood ratio test (McLachlan, 1987) compares two candidates that differ by one class. Data sets are simulated from the smaller candidate and both candidates are re-estimated on each. With B simulated data sets, of which b yield a likelihood ratio at least as large as the observed one, the p-value is (b + 1) / (B + 1) (Davison and Hinkley, 1997); the additional count includes the observed statistic and precludes a p-value of zero from a finite simulation. The p-value is withheld unless every replicate satisfies the estimation checks. The test below compares three and four profiles with three group classes. Nineteen simulated data sets keep the example brief; the smallest attainable p-value is then 1/20 = 0.05, and applied analyses should use at least 99.

smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
#> Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison
#> Null: 3 profiles, 3 group classes; alternative: 4 profiles, 3 group classes
#> Observed statistic: 82.548767
#> p-value: 0.05 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0487) from 19 of 19 valid replicates
plot(test)

Other model types

Latent class models

student_esm contains 2,582 momentary reports from students, with eight activities recorded as present or absent. Declaring the indicators in categorical makes every candidate a latent class model, and the candidates are named with classes in place of profiles.

activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
lca_models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:2,
                                categorical = activities, n_starts = 5,
                                seed = 1)

Among the three-class models, the model with two group classes has the lower BIC. Its relative entropy is 0.56, and its least distinct class has an AvePP of 0.64. The classes of this model overlap substantially, which limits their substantive interpretation.

Single-level models

Observations without a grouping structure are modelled with enumerate_lpa() for continuous indicators and enumerate_lca() for categorical indicators. The candidates are named by their numbers of profiles or classes alone.

srl_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                                   "self_efficacy", "self_regulation",
                                   "test_anxiety"),
                            n_profiles = 1:8, model = "VVI", n_starts = 10,
                            seed = 1)

BIC is minimized by profiles6. The eight-profile candidate has a variance at its lower bound and a nearly empty profile, which marks the limit of what 300 observations can support. The two warnings issued during the enumeration originate from this candidate and are retained in the warnings column of the table.

Missing values and scaled indicators

Two arguments alter the data to which the candidates are fitted and, like n_starts, apply to all candidates. With missing = "fiml", rows with some indicators missing contribute through the indicators observed (full information maximum likelihood); rows with every indicator missing are excluded from the individual sample size, entropy and AvePP, since they carry no information on class membership. centering subtracts and scaling divides by a mean or standard deviation computed over the sample ("grand") or within each group ("person"); combined, they yield grand or within-person z-scores. Information criteria are comparable only among candidates fitted under the same settings. Model selection describes both with examples.

Multiple covariance structures

Specifying several structures in model multiplies the candidates, and the structure is appended to each name. Because the numbers of classes then match several candidates, a candidate must be specified by its full name.

crossed_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies",
                                       "intrinsic_value", "self_efficacy",
                                       "self_regulation", "test_anxiety"),
                                n_profiles = 2:4, model = c("VVI", "EEE"),
                                n_starts = 5, seed = 1)

Latent transition models

With time, every candidate is a latent transition model over the occasions, here the order of each student’s enrolments in sequence. The six-profile model requires more than the default 1,000 EM iterations to meet the convergence tolerance, so max_iter is increased.

transition_models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                                       time = "sequence", n_profiles = 2:6,
                                       n_group_classes = 1, n_starts = 3,
                                       max_iter = 2000, seed = 1)
transition_models

Functions

Call Result
enumerate_classes(data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model) The fitted candidate models
enumerate_classes(…, n_starts = , missing = “fiml”, centering = , scaling = ) The same starts, missing-data handling, centring and scaling for every candidate
enumerate_classes(…, boundary = “exclude”) Starts with a variance at its lower bound set aside for every candidate
as.data.frame(models) One row per candidate with every column
get_results(models, “best”) The candidate at the minimum of each criterion
get_results(models, “classification”) Size, AvePP and entropy of every class of every candidate
get_results(models, “candidates”, cutoff = 0.9) The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff
get_results(models, “deltas”, using = ) Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer
get_results(models, “knees”, using = ) Maximum chord-distance knee of each line, its range and its stability
plot(models), plot(models, what = “bic_groups”), what = “all” Information criteria across the candidates
plot(models, what = “tree”) Division of profiles as more are added
plot(models, what = “entropy”, “avepp” or “diagnostics”, cutoff = ) Entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates
plot(models, what = “deltas”, “heatmap”, “smallest” or “trust”, using = ) Decreases, distance from the lowest criterion, smallest class, estimation checks
plot(models, what = “selection”) All of the plots for choosing the number of classes
get_candidate(models, “profiles4_groups3”), get_candidate(models, 4, 3) One fitted candidate
compare_models(models, “name”, c(4, 2), …) Named candidates side by side
compare_models(models, n_profiles = , n_group_classes = ) All candidates with the given numbers of classes
compare_models(name = fit, name = fit) Fitted models side by side, on the same data
get_candidate(comparison, “name”) The model behind a row of a comparison
get_results(comparison, “classification”) Every class of every compared model
